Kenites
kē´nīts
n. pl. (a nomadic people allied to Israel through Moses' father in law; Hebrew Qeni)
From a root associated with smiths or metalworkers, and with the nest (qen) — a pun Balaam turns on them when he sees their dwelling set in a rock.

Biblical Definition

The Kenites were a tent-dwelling people of the south, bound to Israel not by blood but by kindness. Moses' father in law was of them, and when Israel came up out of Egypt the Kenites shewed them kindness in the wilderness — a mercy God did not forget for four hundred years. The children of the Kenite went up with Judah into the wilderness south of Arad and dwelt among the people; Heber the Kenite severed himself from his kin and pitched his tent by Kedesh, and it was in his tent that Sisera died at Jael's hand. Balaam, looking on them from the heights, took up his parable: “Strong is thy dwellingplace, and thou puttest thy nest in a rock” (Num 24:21). Centuries later, when Saul was sent to destroy Amalek, he first warned the Kenites to depart, “for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel” (1Sa 15:6). The Rechabites, commended by Jeremiah for their obedience, are reckoned of this stock. They are Scripture's standing witness that the God of Israel keeps account of kindness done to His people.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for Kenite; the sense is fixed by the Hebrew text as a people of the south allied to Israel.

expand to see more

The name is not in Webster's 1828 dictionary, which does not treat the Scripture gentilics.

KENITE. A people of Midianite stock, dwelling in the south of Canaan and in the wilderness of Judah.

The tribe of Moses' father in law, variously called Jethro, Reuel, and Hobab.

Their name is connected with the Hebrew for a smith, and by wordplay with qen, a nest.

The Rechabites of Jeremiah 35 are reckoned of the Kenites in 1 Chronicles 2:55.

Key Scripture

Jdg 1:16 — "And the children of the Kenite, Moses' father in law, went up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah into the wilderness of Judah, which lieth in the south of Arad; and they went and dwelt among the people."

Jdg 4:11 — "Now Heber the Kenite, which was of the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses, had severed himself from the Kenites, and pitched his tent unto the plain of Zaanaim, which is by Kedesh."

Num 24:21 — "And he looked on the Kenites, and took up his parable, and said, Strong is thy dwellingplace, and thou puttest thy nest in a rock."

1Sa 15:6 — "And Saul said unto the Kenites, Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel, when they came up out of Egypt. So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps a long account of kindness shewn to His people.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Kenites are too obscure to be fought over, and the danger here is not distortion but neglect — a reader skims the gentilic and misses one of the plainest demonstrations in Scripture of how God remembers.

The principle to recover is the length of the divine memory. Four hundred years separate the kindness shewn in the wilderness from Saul's warning at the edge of the Amalekite slaughter, and the LORD had not forgotten it. Two nations stood side by side in the same country; one had met Israel with a sword and was marked for destruction, the other had met Israel with kindness and was told to depart in peace. The Kenites also show that nearness to the covenant people is a real mercy without being covenant membership: Jael acted for Israel, the Rechabites obeyed their father when Judah would not obey God, and Balaam saw their nest set in a rock. What a man does to the people of God is never lost, in either direction.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Qeni (H7017), Kenite; qen (H7064), a nest; chesed (H2617), kindness, the word used of what they shewed Israel.

expand to see more

Hebrew Qeni (H7017) — a Kenite; Numbers 24:21, Judges 1:16, 1 Samuel 15:6.

Hebrew qen (H7064) — a nest; the wordplay in Balaam's parable, Numbers 24:21.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — kindness, covenant mercy; 1 Samuel 15:6.

Hebrew Chober (H2268) — Heber, the Kenite in whose tent Sisera fell; Judges 4:11.

1 Chronicles 2:55 reckons the house of Rechab among the Kenites.

Usage

"“Ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel” — a mercy remembered four centuries."

"“Thou puttest thy nest in a rock” — Balaam's parable on their dwelling."

"“They went and dwelt among the people” — a stranger folk settled inside Judah."
